newsitem.title: USA: US bonds welcome tame CPI but fear strong economy.
newsitem.headline: US bonds welcome tame CPI but fear strong economy.

text.p: Subdued March U.S. consumer price data heartened financial markets on Tuesday but economic data due over the next two-and-a-half weeks will likely keep investors anxious and limit bond market gains, analysts said.

On Tuesday, the Labor Department reported that the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose just 0.1 percent in March while the core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, rose 0.2 percent. Those gains were smaller than the ones economists had forecast, on average, in a Reuters poll.

In particular, the 0.2 percent rise in the core CPI, coming when some market participants had feared an increase of twice that size, proved a welcome balm for both stock and bond markets, which rallied on the news.

The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrials Average rose close to 100 points in the wake of the consumer price data, and the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond climbed as much as 1-6/32 points before trimming a quarter of that gain.
But analysts said that when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in March, it was not gazing at any current manifestation of inflation.
Rather, monetary policy makers saw a strong economy with a relatively tight labor market and concluded that those factors combined would boost wages and eventually spur inflation.
The Fed "has to be forward-looking and the overall economy still has ample forward momentum," said Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

For instance, U.S. industrial production is forecast at having risen 0.6 percent in March after a 0.5 percent February gain. Economists also believe that the pace of U.S. housing starts probably slowed modestly in March but that the market for new homes remains robust.

Both the housing starts data and the industrial production figures are due on Wednesday. The closely watched Employment Cost Index (ECI) is due at the end of April, and in early May the market faces the April National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index and April U.S. employment data.
For bond prices to rally decisively, investors need clear signs that the economy is "coming off the boil," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
The post-CPI rally "is just a correction in a bear market for bonds" and cannot continue, said Aubrey G. Lanston & Co vice chairman and chief economist David Jones.
Jones said in the weeks and months ahead, the Fed and the market will look at the strength of demand in the economy.

"The Fed is watching indicators of demand, whether it's consumer spending or housing activity or business investment," said Jones. "And all signs show that demand is holding up quite well," he said. "We had a rip-roaring first quarter in terms of strong demand -- paced by the consumer.

"Even if consumer demand moderates in the second quarter, we'll have a lot of strength coming out of the manufacturing sector because business inventories are at record low levels in relation to sales," Jones said.
When inventories are low and demand high, production picks up, bolstering employment and income growth which, in turn, reinforces strong consumer demand, Jones said.
The only offset to this strength is the export side where a strong dollar and weak growth in the European and Japanese economies are hurting demand for U.S. exports, Jones said.

But for bonds "it's the strong demand that really counts," said Jones. "While inflation is moderate at the consumer level, future inflation depends on how strong demand is now," he said. "Particularly given the economy's condition of full employment, that's what the Fed is worried about," he said.
